### An introduction

I am an R&D mathematical statistician working on scientific problems related to all things forest management. The data is often multivariate and longitudinal in space/time, and expensive to collect (i.e., time, labor, resources). It comes from many kinds of studies---designed experiments, observational surveys, and surveys of convenience and opportunity. As such, my work requires broad statistical expertise to meet the needs of many projects and partners.

### The work I do

Most projects involves bread-and-butter statistical and machine learning techniques like [generalized linear mixed models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_mixed_model), [decision trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_tree_learning), and [random forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forest). These are powerful tools that are well understood and perform well when data is small or of modest size.

For the most complex projects I use [Bayesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_statistics) variants of models found in [statistical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics) (e.g., the [Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)). Their interpretation can be done in terms of simple physical systems like circuits and magnets.

For more information, see my [portfolio](portfolio.qmd).

### My training

Before working in forest management R&D, I received my PhD in statistics from [Virginia Tech](https://www.stat.vt.edu) and had postdoctoral fellowships in statistical ecology at [Colorado State University](https://www.biology.colostate.edu/) and [NIMBioS](https://legacy.nimbios.org/) (now [NIMBioS](https://www.nimbios.org/)). As a graduate student, my assistantship was funded by working as a lead statistical collaborator at [LISA (now SAIG)](https://saig.stat.vt.edu/). I also received an [NSF Math-Bio Undergraduate Fellowship](https://math-sites.uncg.edu/math-bio/nsf-fellowship/) as an undergraduate mathematics student at [UNCG](https://mathstats.uncg.edu/).

For more information, see my [CV](cv.qmd).
